name: Brow thread lift

lead: A brow thread lift raises the outer part of the eyebrow using threads placed under the skin, giving a lifted brow and a more open-looking eye area without a surgical brow lift. The lift is visible after the procedure.

The threads are anchored in the brow and forehead tissue to hold the brow tail higher. Surgical lifts reposition tissue through incisions, and botulinum toxin raises the brow by relaxing opposing muscles. No completed trials were found; a registered study plans to examine how long thread-assisted brow suspension lasts.

paras: It is done in a clinic as a minimally invasive procedure and is offered as a middle option between toxin and surgery. How long the lift holds is the open question for people considering it.
Specific complication rates for brow threads were not found. Brow lifts in general carry risks such as infection, bleeding and numbness.

angle.text: Threads are placed to suspend and raise the tail of the brow without surgery, so the brow sits higher and the eye area looks more open once the procedure is done. It is offered as an alternative to surgical brow lifts. Evidence on how long it lasts is thin.

lead: A brow thread lift is a minimally invasive procedure in which threads are placed under the skin to suspend and raise the tail of the eyebrow. People choose it to lift a drooping or low-set brow tail, which opens up the eye area and gives a more alert, youthful look, without the incisions of a surgical brow lift. [1][2]

It sits between injectables and surgery. Wikipedia describes surgical brow lifts, with types including endoscopic, coronal and direct approaches, and non-surgical options such as botulinum toxin, which many patients repeat every four to six months. [1] Thread lifts more broadly use barbed sutures to pull facial skin upward without removing skin. [3]

Published evidence is limited. One registered trial, not yet recruiting as of its listing, plans to examine whether upper blepharoplasty with ligament release improves the durability of thread-assisted brow suspension. [4] A case report has described a vascular complication after a thread brow lift. [5]

paras: Thread-assisted brow suspension uses sutures or threads to hold the brow in a higher position without the incisions of an endoscopic or coronal lift. Surgical brow lifts, by comparison, include endoscopic lifts through small incisions, coronal lifts across the scalp, and direct, mid-forehead, pretrichial, temporal and internal approaches. [1]

The brow sits at the centre of the upper face: the eyebrow carries expression, and its position and shape have been modified cosmetically across history, from hikimayu in Japan to tattooing in the twenty-first century. [2] Brow lifting was first described in the medical literature in the early twentieth century; Wikipedia credits German surgeon Erich Lexer with a 1910 discussion on forehead lifts. [1]

Botulinum toxin injections can raise the brow temporarily and are repeated every four to six months. [1] Absorbable Endotine implants have been used in surgical lifts, though they may not support very thick forehead tissue or heavy brows. [1]

Surgical brow lifts are described as having rare, usually minor complications in trained hands, including numbness, hair loss or hairline change, infection and bleeding. [1] Thread lifts in general can leave threads in the skin, so problems can be hard to reverse; a physician quoted by the BBC called thread lifts among the more hazardous aesthetic procedures, and a BBC investigation of a training course reported poor infection control. [3]
A 2023 case report described an arteriovenous fistula of the superficial temporal vessels after a thread brow lift. [5]

A registered interventional trial (NCT07879456) with a planned 90 participants will assess durability of thread-assisted brow suspension combined with ligament release during upper blepharoplasty, in people with brow ptosis and dermatochalasis; it is listed as not yet recruiting. [4] No results are available. Published human data otherwise consist of case reports. [5]

timeline.event: Erich Lexer writes the first documented medical discussion of a forehead lift, according to Wikipedia. [1]
